sources.news_title: US and Iran Reportedly Discuss Phased Deal to Reopen Hormuz
sources.text:
US and Iranian negotiators are considering a phased cease-fire agreement that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz and lead Washington to lift its economic blockade against Tehran, according to multiple reports.
Representatives of the two countries met on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday to discuss a framework resembling the memorandum of understanding reached in mid-June, sources told Reuters.
The negotiating teams reportedly believe a step-by-step agreement may be the only path forward, as neither side is willing to give up its leverage before the other.
“One way forward would be to solve the crisis in stages. The first would be to end the blockade and reopen Hormuz,” a senior Iranian official told Reuters.
A US official told The Post that the discussions had been “positive” and “constructive,” adding that Washington was negotiating from a position of strength while continuing to escort ships through the Strait of Hormuz.
Although senior Iranian officials have publicly ruled out concessions to the United States, a White House official said Tehran’s willingness to negotiate indicated that the country was feeling the economic impact of the US blockade and sanctions.
“Iran is desperate for a deal, President Trump holds all the cards and will make whatever decision is best for the United States,” the US official said.
MORE ON THIS: Alleged Mistress Alleigha Botner Testifies in Caleb Flynn Case
Iranian officials rejected that assessment, saying Tehran was prepared for every possible outcome, including war, if negotiations fail to produce an agreement.
“Our fingers are on the trigger,” an Iranian official told Reuters. “The Americans know what they need to do but, because of their excessive demands, the chances of diplomacy resolving this are extremely low.”
The talks followed comments from Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who told reporters in New York that he had proposed a new, seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the United States met certain conditions.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian also said the strategic waterway would remain closed until US sanctions and the naval blockade were lifted.
Trump, meanwhile, warned earlier this week that he could choose to “annihilate” Iran as peace negotiations appeared to be faltering.
Despite the threats and recent Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, reports of potential peace negotiations helped ease a sharp rise in oil prices on Friday.
Brent crude futures fell 1.1% to $105.46 on Friday morning, while West Texas Intermediate declined by a similar percentage to $93.56.
With Post wires

sources.news_title: NEW: Iran, U.S. Discussing 'Phased Approach' To Fully Re-Open Strait of Hormuz In Matter Of Days
sources.text:
Politics
NEW: Iran, U.S. Discussing ‘Phased Approach’ To Fully Re-Open Strait of Hormuz In Matter Of Days
The United States and Iran are discussing a phased arrangement that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz to full commercial traffic within days if agreed conditions are met, according to officials and sources familiar with talks held on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi announced Friday that Tehran had conveyed a seven-day plan through Qatar. “Iran has conveyed to the United States, through Qatar, a concrete seven-day plan. If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, and normal maritime passage restored within seven days,” Araghchi said. “The choice now rests with the United States.”
He added, “If certain conditions are met, the strait will be open within seven days and talks will start.” Araghchi further stated that the proposal was “not new” and largely falls in line with the short-lived memorandum of understanding that was agreed to earlier this year.
One senior Iranian official described the approach as sequential. “One way forward would be to solve the crisis in stages. The first would be to end the blockade and reopen Hormuz,” the official told Reuters on condition of anonymity.
The June memorandum, which was signed by President Donald Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, called for an immediate end to military operations on all fronts, U.S. removal of a naval blockade beginning at signing and completed within 30 days, and Iranian arrangements for safe commercial passage “with no charge for 60 days only.”

The text stated that traffic “will immediately start, and considering the need for removing the technical and military obstacles and demining by the Islamic Republic of Iran, will be instated within 30 days.” The memorandum also provided for oil-export waivers and 60 days of talks toward a final agreement. That arrangement later collapsed amid mutual accusations of non-implementation.
Pezeshkian said Iran preferred a return to that framework before U.S. congressional elections in November. “We don’t want it to get to the midterm elections,” he said. “We wish Americans to return to the MOU before the midterms.”
He added, “We did reach an agreement with your president, that agreement was signed, and based on that, we are willing and still wish to move forward.”
A U.S. official described current contacts as “positive and constructive” while stating that Washington was not in a rush, citing continued oil movements under U.S. escort. A White House official said President Trump “holds all the cards and will make whatever decision is best for the United States,” remained “open to talking with Iran under the right circumstances,” and viewed the United States as being in “a very strong position.”
Special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have participated in mediated exchanges with Iranian officials in New York, though no agreement has been reached as of this report.

sources.text:
France is working on a draft United Nations Security Council resolution backing freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, a U.N. diplomat said Friday.
The resolution would reaffirm the need to respect freedom of navigation in the strait, a flashpoint in the war in Iran, citing its importance for global shipments critical for food and energy security, the diplomat said, speaking on condition of anonymity because discussions on the measure have been private.
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia’s top cleric issued a rare statement, calling on the kingdom’s troops to defend the country from neighboring Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
In New York, where the wars in Iran and Gaza have dominated the U.N. agenda, the leaders of Iraq, Lebanon and Egypt were scheduled to address world leaders later Friday.
Here is a look at the latest news from the Middle East. More coverage of the U.N. General Assembly is available here.
France overseeing new UN draft proposal to reopen strait
The proposed U.N. resolution would recall the need to respect the Law of the Sea and support peaceful initiatives aimed at ensuring safe passage in the strait, the U.N. diplomat said.
Iran’s disruption of the strait, through which a fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas transited before the war, has emerged as its main point of leverage. The effects have been felt far beyond the Middle East and pose political problems for U.S. President Donald Trump and his Republican Party ahead of November’s midterm congressional elections.
Trump and French President Emmanuel Macron discussed the topic on the sidelines of this week’s annual U.N. gathering of global leaders, the diplomat said. It also was discussed with Arab nations and Iran.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi confirmed Friday that Tehran put forth a seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume talks on its nuclear program if the U.S. meets the conditions it has laid out.
Talking to reporters at the U.N., Araghchi said the plan was delivered to Washington through Qatari mediators on the sidelines of the General Assembly.
“If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days,” he said, adding that seven-day clock would begin when the U.S. accepts the plan. “The choice now rests with the United States.”
The White House said earlier Friday that U.S. officials are having positive and constructive conversations with mediators on the Iran war
Top religious figure urges Saudi troops to be ready to defend kingdom
With Saudi oil facilities, cities and ships off its coast coming under escalating attacks, the kingdom's top religious authority has called on soldiers to be prepared to defend the country from Iran-backed Houthis.
Grand Mufti Sheikh Saleh al-Fawzan, who traditionally avoids weighing in on politics in a country that holds enormous influence among Muslims worldwide, issued the strongly worded statement. Al-Fawzan addressed his message to soldiers defending the kingdom's borders and members of the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen, peppering it with Quranic verses and religious edicts.
“Protecting this great nation, guarding its borders, defending against aggression and punishing those who want to harm any inch of it is one of the greatest duties,” he said.
The head of Yemen's internationally recognized government, Rashad al-Alimi, likewise urged Yemenis to rally behind Saudi-backed armed forces and allied groups in their fight with the Houthis.
Al-Alimi, who chairs the country’s Presidential Leadership Council, also called on Yemenis fighting alongside the Houthis to defect, announcing a general amnesty.
Al-Alimi says goal is to retake capital Sanaa from Houthis
Al-Alimi said the aim of the fighting is to restore his government’s control over Sanaa, the capital, which the Houthis seized in 2014.
His call to arms came during his first speech since his Saudi-backed forces were routed from the western Red Sea coast by the Houthis’ lightning advance on the city of Mokha and islands in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, where 12% of the world's trade passes.
The swift Houthi advances raised questions about the effectiveness of the Saudi-backed forces in the face of the disciplined, well-armed Houthis. The Houthi assault exploited divisions among the Saudi-backed forces and distrust among its leaders, leading to a chaotic troop withdrawal before the fall of Mokha.
Al-Alimi’s speech came on the 64th anniversary of the military coup that ousted the monarchy ruling northern Yemen, rooted in the Zaydi Shiite sect to which the Houthis also belong. The Houthis battled Yemen’s central government for years before sweeping down from their northern stronghold and seizing Sanaa.
Pakistani, Saudi and Turkish military chiefs hold first joint meeting
The first joint meeting of the military chiefs of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey was held in Riyadh on Friday, following the signing of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement by the three countries, Pakistan’s military said in a statement.
The chiefs of defense forces and chiefs of general staff from the three countries reviewed the regional security situation and threats facing Saudi Arabia, according to the statement.
“They strongly resented the attacks targeting the Holy City of Mecca and civilian and economic infrastructure,” the statement said.
The military chiefs also praised the vigilance and professionalism of the Saudi armed forces in ensuring the safety of the people and security of the kingdom, it said.
Iran's president says he supports Xi's call for return to MOA
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Friday in a post on X that Tehran supports Chinese President Xi Jinping’s call for a return to the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding and renewed diplomacy between Iran and the United States.
Pezeshkian said he appreciated Xi’s “thoughtful and responsible support” for resolving differences through dialogue and diplomacy, adding that Iran backed returning to the understanding and honoring previously agreed commitments.
The post came a day after Pezeshkian met with Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York. Sharif said Pezeshkian told him the Islamabad memorandum remained “fully acceptable” to Iran and that Tehran was ready to take it forward.
The 14-point memorandum, mediated by Pakistan and signed in June, provided a framework for ending the conflict.
UN Security Council demands halt to attacks by Houthi rebels
In a statement approved by its 15 members, the U.N.’s most powerful body condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and against commercial shipping in the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The council called for “practical cooperation,” including with Yemen’s internationally recognized government, to prevent the Houthis from obtaining weapons, military material and training enabling them to carry out attacks.
It reminded all countries of their obligation to implement the U.N. arms embargo against the Houthis.
2 Israeli soldiers are killed in Gaza
Israel’s military said two of its soldiers were killed in northern Gaza on Thursday while inspecting an unexploded Israeli drone near a military post. They were the first Israeli soldiers killed in Gaza in months.
Five other Israeli soldiers have been killed since last October’s ceasefire that attempted to halt a more than two-year war between Israel and the militant Hamas group.
While the heaviest fighting has subsided, almost daily Israeli fire has continued. Israeli forces have carried out repeated airstrikes and frequently fire on Palestinians near military-held zones and have killed 1,408 Palestinians, according to Gaza health officials.
This report will be updated throughout the day as new developments emerge.

sources.news_title: IRAN-U.S. TALKS ENTER TECHNICAL PHASE AS LAWMAKERS PRESS FOR ANSWERS ON CHINA, RUSSIA AND FENTANYL
sources.text:
Negotiations between the United States and Iran have moved beyond initial diplomatic contacts into a more detailed technical phase, according to Al Jazeera's bureau chief in Tehran, Nourddine Dgheir, who reported Friday that sources in the Iranian capital described the atmosphere around the talks as increasingly positive.
The account, carried by the breaking-news account @FirstSquawk, followed an earlier bulletin from the same account stating that Iran-U.S. talks had entered a technical stage. The reported shift comes as other outlets describe a wider diplomatic push: The New York Times reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio said U.S. negotiators had restarted conversations about Iran's nuclear program, while adding that there had been no breakthroughs. The Times also reported that Iran has proposed a seven-day plan under which the Strait of Hormuz would reopen and nuclear talks would be revived.
Iran's president, Masoud Pezeshkian, has said Tehran wants a deal with the United States before November's midterm elections, according to accounts of his exchange with news organizations. The same reporting stated that Pezeshkian described meeting twice with the Islamic Republic's new supreme leader, who has not been seen in public. A separate assessment published by the Institute for the Study of War noted that Iran's deteriorating economy and its difficulties exerting control over the Strait of Hormuz may have contributed to its willingness to engage with Washington.
Against that backdrop, the reaction inside the United States is being carried less by the State Department than by lawmakers who say any warming of relations must be weighed against the conduct of America's other adversaries — and against China, the country Washington simultaneously calls its biggest strategic competitor.
On Newsmax's "National Report," Representative Greg Steube, a Florida Republican, was asked about the just-concluded three-day state visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping and what it accomplished. He said the most significant outcome was a two-month pause on trade measures, which he described as helpful to Midwestern farmers at a time when they are being squeezed by pricing, diesel and fertilizer costs. He added that many subjects were not discussed openly, naming Iran, Taiwan and the flow of fentanyl precursors into Mexico as matters he hopes were addressed behind closed doors.
"Them not cooperating with Iran or Russia on military type things, the fentanyl precursors is obviously huge," @Newsmax quoted Steube as saying. In the accompanying transcript, Steube pointed to an interview that had aired earlier in the program, in which he said an ambassador had made clear that China should not be helping Iran with targeting, with oil, or with military capabilities. "So hopefully that's going to be the case and that's not going to happen," he said.
Pressed on what he wants the president to secure from Beijing before the trade truce expires, Steube put national security first. "Well, obviously good trade relations with them are very important. But on the national security front them not cooperating with Iran or Russia on military type things," he said, calling the fentanyl precursor issue enormous and noting that hundreds of thousands of Americans have died of fentanyl overdoses. He said the precursors come into Mexico for the cartels, and that the president has said going back years that he has asked China not to sell them into Mexico. On trade, Steube said the United States should not run a deficit with China and argued that decades of what he called bad trade policy made China wealthy. "We have to get that right," he said, adding that a two-month window helps farmers but that longer-lasting agreements are needed.
The program then turned to the visit's closing stop: the National Archives, where the Chinese president and President Trump were to tour the Constitution and the Bill of Rights. Steube called the setting interesting, noting that the country is marking its two hundred fiftieth anniversary and that letting the Chinese see where America comes from — how it was founded and what values it stands on — matters in bilateral relations. The host remarked that the feed from the room was poor and that he was almost positive he heard "Stand by Me" playing in the background, a bit of color he acknowledged he might have imagined.
Steube also responded to a sound bite from State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott, who said the president has put the United States in position to make things at home again, that trillions in investment are returning in large part because of tariffs, and that Washington wants deals that are wins for both sides. Steube agreed, citing the tax-cut package Republicans passed to incentivize manufacturing to return to the United States. "We have to have that here and we have to put America first," he said.
Separately, Reuters reported that Russia's Perm oil refinery halted operations after a drone attack on Friday, according to sources — a reminder that the energy and security file extends well beyond the Iran talks.
What is being described here is a reported diplomatic opening and the political reaction to it. The claim that the Iran-U.S. talks have advanced into a technical phase rests on the Al Jazeera bureau chief's sourcing in Tehran as relayed by @FirstSquawk, not on any announcement by either government. The proposed seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and revive nuclear talks comes from the reporting of The New York Times, and the description of positive atmosphere and Iranian interest in a pre-midterm deal comes from that outlet and from Pezeshkian's own remarks as reported. No text, joint statement or formal terms of a technical agreement have been released publicly. Next News Network could not independently verify the claims about the status and tone of the negotiations.
The reaction has spread through a recognizable set of channels: Newsmax carried Steube's television comments and posted them through @Newsmax; @FirstSquawk relayed the Al Jazeera reporting and the earlier technical-stage bulletin; Reuters carried the Perm refinery disruption; and the broader diplomatic picture has been documented by The New York Times and the Institute for the Study of War. Each of those accounts is carrying its own portion of the story, and none of them constitutes confirmation of the others.
Our Take
Two things can be true at once, and conservatives should hold both. It is not weakness to talk to Tehran if the alternative is a wider war, and the reported reopening of the Strait of Hormuz would relieve pressure on global energy prices that American families feel at the pump and on the farm. But there is no deal yet, and the only thing being described so far is an atmosphere. An atmosphere is not a verification regime, a nuclear inspection schedule, or an enforcement mechanism — and the fact that Tehran's apparent motive is its own deteriorating economy and its shaky grip on the Strait should tell us who needs this more.
Steube's point deserves more attention than the diplomatic headlines getting the airtime. If Washington is simultaneously easing trade pressure on Beijing for two months while asking Iran to disarm, the China file cannot be an afterthought: fentanyl precursors are still crossing into Mexico, and Beijing's willingness to help Iran on targeting, oil or military capability is the variable that decides whether any Iran deal holds. Trade peace with a strategic competitor should buy American farmers relief and American security a harder line — not one at the expense of the other. Republicans should insist that any Iran agreement, before an election-year signing ceremony, be judged by what is verifiable, not by what is said to be positive.

sources.news_title: US, Iran explore phased deal to end conflict as Hormuz, economic sanctions become bargaining chips
sources.text:
US, Iran explore phased deal to end conflict as Hormuz, economic sanctions become bargaining chips
Mail This Article
US and Iranian negotiators in New York are exploring a phased path out of war that would involve Tehran reopening the Strait of Hormuz and Washington lifting its economic blockade of Iran.
The strait has become the central bargaining chip in efforts to end the nearly seven-month US-Iran conflict, with Iran seeking relief from the US blockade that is choking its economy and Washington seeking free passage for ships on the global oil supply route now blocked by Tehran, according to sources close to the talks.
The talks face a big obstacle as neither side wants to be the first to surrender its leverage, according to comments to Reuters by two Iranian sources, two regional officials and two Western diplomatic sources, but behind Iran's stance is a recognition of the economic cost of prolonged confrontation.
A senior Iranian official said the most plausible way to end the impasse would be a phased arrangement, with Iran allowing navigation through Hormuz in return for the US lifting its economic blockade and Tehran potentially gaining access to frozen assets.
"One way forward would be to solve the crisis in stages. The first would be to end the blockade and reopen Hormuz," he said on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
That would involve US President Donald Trump accepting another temporary fix, after an earlier understanding collapsed in July. So a central challenge facing the negotiators is not just to sketch out a deal but also to ensure any concessions are durable enough for both sides to trust, the sources said.
Trump has said he thinks the US and Iran could reach a deal after midterm elections to Congress on November 3. A senior European official said the Iranians "have a very long list of demands."
A White House official said that while "Iran is desperate for a deal, President Trump holds all the cards and will make whatever decision is best for the United States." Trump, he said, remained "open to talking with Iran under the right circumstances" but had no need to negotiate, and the US was in a "very strong position" with control of the Strait of Hormuz and an Iranian economy that was "collapsing."
The official said "crushing sanctions" and "one of the most successful blockades in history" have crippled Iran’s economy and left Iran completely broke. Trump was content to let the "inevitable Iranian collapse" play out rather than be "played" by Tehran, the official said.
A deal before the midterms could benefit Trump, as reopening Hormuz could ease tensions in the Gulf, contain oil prices and help bring down politically sensitive US gasoline prices.
Iran's chances of gaining much-needed economic relief may be greater while Trump still has a greater political incentive to strike a bargain.
Leverage as obstacle?
 The leverage that brought Washington and Tehran back to negotiations could also make compromise harder.
Washington controls the pressure that is hurting Tehran most, while Tehran controls access to a critical energy chokepoint. Neither side wants to surrender that leverage without extracting something tangible in return.
This means the midterms may be less a deadline for diplomacy than for preserving the conditions that make the diplomatic efforts possible. If Washington and Tehran cannot turn leverage into a deal before the midterms, the diplomatic window could narrow as the risk of escalation grows.

There is considerably more diplomacy underway than there was a week ago, but the negotiations have so far produced another roadmap rather than an agreement.

Etihad Rail has launched a new freight service linking Fujairah, on the Gulf of Oman outside the Strait of Hormuz, with Abu Dhabi’s industrial center roughly 200 kilometers away, with container trains running three times a week and customs clearance available at the Abu Dhabi end. The route gives importers another way to bring cargo into the UAE without sending ships through Hormuz, where traffic has been heavily disrupted since the Iran war began. The rail connection also adds another piece to the infrastructure already clustered around Fujairah, including ADNOC’s 1.5 million bpd Habshan Fujairah crude pipeline and the emirate’s large oil storage and bunkering complex. US and Iran discuss phased deal to reopen Hormuz and end US blockade, sources say
- By Reuters -
- Sep 25, 2026
US and Iranian negotiators in New York are exploring a phased path out of war that would involve Tehran reopening the Strait of Hormuz and Washington lifting its economic blockade of Iran, sources close to the talks said.
The strait has become the central bargaining chip in efforts to end the nearly seven-month US-Iran conflict, with Iran seeking relief from the US blockade that is choking its economy and Washington seeking free passage for ships on the global oil supply route now blocked by Tehran.
The talks face a big obstacle as neither side wants to be the first to surrender its leverage, according to comments to Reuters by two Iranian sources, two regional officials and two Western diplomatic sources, but behind Iran’s stance is a recognition of the economic cost of prolonged confrontation.
A senior Iranian official said the most plausible way to end the impasse would be a phased arrangement, with Iran allowing navigation through Hormuz in return for the US lifting its economic blockade and Tehran potentially gaining access to frozen assets.
“One way forward would be to solve the crisis in stages. The first would be to end the blockade and reopen Hormuz,” he said on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
That would involve US President Donald Trump accepting another temporary fix, after an earlier understanding collapsed in July. So a central challenge facing the negotiators is not just to sketch out a deal but also to ensure any concessions are durable enough for both sides to trust, the sources said.
Trump has said he thinks the US and Iran could reach a deal after midterm elections to Congress on November 3. A senior European official said the Iranians “have a very long list of demands.”
A White House official said that while “Iran is desperate for a deal, President Trump holds all the cards and will make whatever decision is best for the United States.”
Trump, he said, remained “open to talking with Iran under the right circumstances” but had no need to negotiate, and the US was in a “very strong position” with control of the Strait of Hormuz and an Iranian economy that was “collapsing.”
The official said “crushing sanctions” and “one of the most successful blockades in history” have crippled Iran’s economy and left Iran completely broke. Trump was content to let the “inevitable Iranian collapse” play out rather than be “played” by Tehran, the official said.
Former US negotiator Dennis Ross said he saw only a 30% chance of an agreement being reached before the vote, but that both sides may have stronger reasons to make a deal before than after the midterms.
“The blockade is what’s really squeezing the Iranians. It’s strangling them,” Ross said.
A deal before the midterms could benefit Trump, as reopening Hormuz could ease tensions in the Gulf, contain oil prices and help bring down politically sensitive US gasoline prices.
Iran’s chances of gaining much-needed economic relief may be greater while Trump still has a greater political incentive to strike a bargain.
After the midterms, Ross said, Trump may face fewer constraints and be more willing to intensify pressure or consider military options.
LEVERAGE AS OBSTACLE?
The leverage that brought Washington and Tehran back to negotiations could also make compromise harder.
Washington controls the pressure that is hurting Tehran most, while Tehran controls access to a critical energy chokepoint. Neither side wants to surrender that leverage without extracting something tangible in return.
This means the midterms may be less a deadline for diplomacy than for preserving the conditions that make the diplomatic efforts possible. If Washington and Tehran cannot turn leverage into a deal before the midterms, the diplomatic window could narrow as the risk of escalation grows.

Even as it seeks a diplomatic off-ramp, Tehran is preparing for the possibility of renewed war with Washington, the Iranian official said, accusing the US of using the economic blockade and threat of force as tools of coercion.
“Our fingers are on the trigger,” said the senior Iranian official. “The Americans know what they need to do but, because of their excessive demands, the chances of diplomacy resolving this are extremely low.”
Regional sources said Tehran was willing to drop a demand for payment of transit fees to use the Strait of Hormuz from the main agreement and put the demand in a side attachment instead, as ending the blockade had become the more urgent priority.
Gulf states have rejected the proposal for payment of transit fees. Any arrangement would be temporary, not a formal abandonment of Iran’s position, the regional sources said.
The US has tightened the economic vice on Iran, layering new sanctions on top of a blockade that has choked off Iran’s oil exports, an important source of hard currency.
This month, it targeted Iran’s remaining commercial airlines and support networks as part of a campaign to sever the economic lifelines sustaining the government and the powerful Revolutionary Guards. Trump warned that Iran’s economy could “rot” unless it reached a deal.
“Iran is not primarily focused on imposing tolls in Hormuz but on preserving its administrative control of the waterway,” he said. “Iran may be willing to defer the toll issue, but they are not going to give up administrative control of the strait.”
At the heart of the diplomacy in New York is a fundamental tension. Washington wants pressure to produce concessions, Tehran wants pressure removed before making them, and the Gulf states want the conflict resolved without allowing the region’s strategic waterways to become enduring bargaining chips.
FEARS OF AN OPEN-ENDED CONFLICT
During a separate meeting with Trump in New York, Gulf leaders sought clarity on Washington’s endgame beyond the midterms, including on whether the US would resume military action if Iran refused to return to negotiations.
They conveyed their collective rejection of any Iranian control of Hormuz, saying freedom of navigation must be restored and that the strategic waterway should not become a tool of coercion against Gulf states, regional sources said.
Yet alongside their warnings over Hormuz, Gulf leaders have pressed hard for de-escalation and a political process, reflecting the region’s determination to stay out of any further conflict between the US and Iran.
“It’s still not clear what Trump’s endgame is, or what the alternative to the pressure campaign would be,” said Ebtessam al-Ketbi, president of the Emirates Policy Center think tank based in Abu Dhabi.
“The Iranians, by contrast, know what they want. They’re reshaping the regional landscape through Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb with a clear objective while Washington has yet to define its roadmap,” she said, referring to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
That uncertainty is also shaping Tehran’s calculations. Danny Citrinowicz, a regional analyst and former Israeli military intelligence officer, said the New York talks had not altered the basic positions of either side and that Iran was unlikely to retreat as long as it believed Trump wanted to avoid a wider escalation before the midterms.
“The blockade is hurting them, but rather than softening their position, it is likely to drive them to escalate because they believe that if they soften their position, they are dead,” said Alan Eyre, a former US negotiator on Iran.
A Western official familiar with the talks added: “It is all about opening the Strait of Hormuz. We’re all under pressure domestically and the Iranians know that.”

sources.news_title: Iran presents US with roadmap to end the war
sources.text:
Iran has presented the US with a roadmap to end the war that echoes the two countries’ June agreement — a 60-day ceasefire, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and groundwork for further talks — The National reported. The initiative follows US-Iran talks that President Donald Trump said had momentum, with Qatar, Pakistan, and, increasingly, Egypt mediating. It also comes at a time of military posturing, heated rhetoric, and signs that other actors are muddying the waters. China has sent Iran around 1,300 shipments containing “dual-use” components for drones and missile guidance systems, The Wall Street Journal reported.
Gulf states want de-escalation, but are seeking their own talks with Tehran rather than relying solely on the US-Iran framework. Economic interdependence with Iran could anchor regional security, Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed Al Ansari argued at the Concordia Annual Summit in New York.
Expectations aren’t high: Former Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Hamad bin Jassim warned that temporary solutions favor Tehran’s strategy of patience. To counter that, Gulf countries “must bear some of the pain too, and insist on reaching a legal, permanent, and clear solution for the issue of the Strait of Hormuz.”

sources.news_title: Iran offers 60-day ceasefire plan as Hormuz tensions remain high
sources.text:
Diplomatic efforts between Washington and Tehran continued on Thursday, September 24, 208 days after the war began, as tensions over the Strait of Hormuz remained high.
Tehran has presented Washington with a roadmap proposing a region-wide ceasefire of up to 60 days, a phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and a timetable for broader negotiations to end the conflict, Gulf News reported, citing regional sources briefed on the proposal.
The proposal reportedly also includes a halt to attacks on Arab neighbours. Iranian officials have previously said the strategic waterway could be reopened within seven days if Washington meets Tehran’s conditions.
Iranian officials in New York said diplomacy remained possible, but any agreement would have to address Tehran’s demands, including the lifting of the US naval blockade of Iranian ports. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also indicated that Washington remains open to diplomacy while maintaining that military options remain available.
Iran sets conditions for negotiations
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said Tehran would not return to previous arrangements and that its conditions were now different.
“Until our conditions are met, the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened and we will not negotiate,” Rezaei said, according to state-run IRNA.
He said Washington must act first to restore the trust of the Iranian people before Tehran would consider negotiations.
Shipping through Hormuz remains limited
Preliminary data showed that 10 cargo ships crossed the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, up from seven the previous day. The figure remained below the 10-day moving average of about 17 vessels.
The data may be revised because some vessels switch off their transponders during voyages.
US Central Command said its forces had redirected 115 commercial vessels as of September 23 while enforcing what it calls America’s “steel wall blockade”.
Oil prices ease
Oil prices fell on Thursday after rising about 4 per cent in the previous session, following indications that Iran remained open to diplomacy.
Brent crude futures fell 94 cents, or 0.9 per cent, to USD 102.13 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate crude declined 59 cents, or 0.7 per cent, to USD 91.56 a barrel.
Iran warns neighbours over flights
Iran has warned neighbouring countries against helping the US restrict Iranian flights, with Rezaei threatening action against airports that cooperate with Washington.
The warning followed US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s statement that Iranian airlines would face measures aimed at stopping their international operations from September 23 through secondary sanctions on aviation service providers.
Bessent told Fox News that more than 80 per cent or 90 per cent of international flights from Iran had been suspended.
Bessent outlines US strategy
Bessent said the Trump administration’s strategy could result in divisions within Iran’s leadership, an uprising by the Iranian people or an agreement under which Tehran would honour its commitments.
On tanker traffic, he said most vessels continued to sail despite reports of ships being targeted. He also warned companies and financial institutions supporting Iran that they would face US enforcement action.
Tehran criticises Canada’s Carney
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei criticised Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney over his remarks on the conflict.
In a post on X, Baghaei accused Carney of portraying a threat to “annihilate Iran” as merely “the language of war”.
He also criticised countries that he said had relied on US pressure, accusing them of sacrificing their independence.
Pezeshkian rejects using Hormuz as leverage
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told the UN General Assembly (UNGA) that Tehran would not allow the Strait of Hormuz to be used as leverage against Iran.
“We cannot let some have free access and bolster their interests from the waterway, while at the same time using that waterway to impose their aggression upon us,” he said.
UAE bars Bank Melli
The UAE central bank has barred Iran’s Bank Melli from operating in the country, Reuters reported, citing breaches of regulatory requirements.
The move follows the UAE’s decision in August to suspend trade, commercial exchanges and financial transactions with Iran until further notice.
Eight suicide attempts reported among US personnel
The Trump administration has acknowledged eight suicide attempts involving US service members during the extended deployment of the USS Abraham Lincoln, according to information disclosed by Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao.
The figure was included in a letter responding to questions from Democratic Senator Kirsten Gillibrand about conditions aboard the aircraft carrier, AFP reported.
The disclosure comes amid scrutiny in the US over conditions and mental health among personnel during the prolonged deployment.

sources.news_title: New York Contacts Revive Hopes for US-Iran Talks
sources.text:
Intensive contacts in New York on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly meetings have revived hopes of breaking the deadlock in US-Iran negotiations, as Tehran presented Washington with an official proposal outlining specific conditions for resuming talks and discussions emerged about a phased process to end the war.
A US official said Washington had held constructive discussions with Tehran through intermediaries, confirming that nuclear issues were still being discussed.
In New York, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran had presented Washington with a plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to maritime traffic within seven days, alongside discussions on the conditions for ending the war and reopening the vital waterway.
On Tuesday, Araghchi met with US President Donald Trump’s envoy, Steve Witkoff, after setting conditions for ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
In the same context, Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani said Doha held indirect talks between Tehran and Washington on Thursday and made progress, noting that Qatar had sensed a willingness on both sides to advance the negotiations.
Sheikh Mohammed called for an end to the use of waterways as a means of pressuring countries and imposing faits accomplis, describing the situation in the Strait of Hormuz as unacceptable.
He said the blockade imposed on the Strait of Hormuz was putting pressure on Iran and also placing pressure on countries across the region, noting that developments in the strait were not affecting Tehran alone but the entire world.
He added that Qatar had made efforts to put the diplomatic process back on the right track.
As part of regional efforts, Araghchi met with his Saudi counterpart, Prince Faisal bin Farhan, on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
Araghchi briefed him on the understanding reached between Tehran and the Sultanate of Oman regarding safe maritime corridors in the Strait of Hormuz.
He affirmed Iran’s determination to build confidence, particularly regarding security mechanisms based on cooperation among regional countries, expressing hope that key regional parties would participate in these efforts.
Araghchi also met with Arab League Secretary-General Nabil El-Sisi and discussed regional developments, particularly the situations in Palestine and Lebanon.
He reaffirmed Tehran’s determination to strengthen confidence among regional countries, calling for intensified dialogue and communication between Iran and Arab states. He said regional security should be viewed as an integrated concept based on shared responsibility and constructive engagement.
The Arab League secretary-general expressed hope that regional efforts and an expanded dialogue would help strengthen trust and cooperation among the countries of the region.
In earlier remarks several days ago, the Qatari prime minister said energy was a source of strength for his country and diversification was the foundation of its resilience, while technology represented its future. He stressed that Qatar would not allow short-term disruptions to determine its trajectory despite the prevailing uncertainty.
He added that Qatar was moving forward by investing in reform, strengthening its resilience and creating new opportunities for growth, stressing that it would remain a committed partner in mediation, a reliable energy supplier and an investment partner.
He also said Qatar’s financial system had continued to operate and that companies had continued their activities despite what had occurred.
Source: Agencies

sources.news_title: Brent Rose 3.4% as Hormuz Deal Talk Hit. Traders Price a 30 September Reopening at 0.25%
sources.text:
Oil traders spent Thursday repricing every new headline out of the Gulf, but prediction-market traders are still giving almost no chance that normal traffic through the Strait of Hormuz returns by the end of September.
Brent settled September 24 at $106.60 a barrel, up 3.4%, while West Texas Intermediate gained 2.7% to $94.61. That was a sharp move from the $103.67 Brent price in FinanceFeeds’ September 24 look at the $74 million Kharg Island prediction market, published earlier that morning.
The new development came later Thursday, when Reuters reported that U.S. and Iranian negotiators in New York were exploring a phased agreement under which Tehran would reopen Hormuz and Washington would lift its economic blockade of Iran. The report arrived after crude had risen as much as about 5% on renewed supply fears following Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, and prices subsequently pulled back from those session highs.
The Deal Being Discussed Starts With Hormuz
Reuters cited two Iranian sources, two regional officials and two Western diplomatic sources in reporting that negotiators were examining a staged route out of the nearly seven-month conflict.
A senior Iranian official described the first stage as ending the U.S. blockade and reopening Hormuz, potentially alongside access to frozen Iranian assets. Reuters said neither side wants to surrender its principal source of leverage first: Washington controls the economic pressure on Iran, while Tehran controls access to the critical shipping route.
Bloomberg separately reported that Qatari officials were mediating the negotiations.
The discussions build on an Iranian offer first reported on Tuesday, September 22, rather than a new seven-day proposal made Thursday. A senior Iranian official told Reuters that day that Tehran could reopen Hormuz within seven days if Washington eased military pressure and lifted its blockade on Iranian ports.
Iran’s position hardened again on Friday. A senior Iranian official told Reuters on September 25 that the strait would remain closed until “all of Iran’s conditions are met” and said Tehran would make no concessions over its nuclear rights even if Washington accepted the Hormuz proposal.
Polymarket Has Nearly Written Off September 30
The prediction market is assigning very different odds to the timetable.
At 15:30 UTC on September 25, Polymarket’s contract asking whether Strait of Hormuz traffic would return to normal by September 30 priced “Yes” at just 0.25%, with $411,533 traded over the previous 24 hours.
The October 31 contract was at 8.5% on $67,145 of 24-hour volume. Later Friday, Polymarket was still displaying the September contract below 1% and the October market at roughly 8%.
The contracts use a specific definition of “normal”: IMF PortWatch must publish a seven-day moving average of at least 60 transit calls through Hormuz before the relevant deadline.
That makes the prediction-market question much stricter than whether Iran announces an agreement or allows several tankers through. Traders are betting on restored traffic, not simply a diplomatic headline.
The Saudi Bypass Gets Much Better Odds
The contrast with Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline is striking.
At the same 15:30 UTC Polymarket read, the contract asking whether the pipeline would restart by October 31 was priced at 75.4% “Yes.” The line gives Saudi Arabia a route from its eastern oil fields to the Red Sea that avoids Hormuz entirely.
That alternative has already mattered for crude pricing. FinanceFeeds reported on September 18 that Brent fell toward $102 as Saudi Arabia moved to restore part of the damaged East-West Pipeline.
Reuters subsequently reported on September 22 that pumping had restarted at a reduced rate, although full capacity could take several more weeks to restore.
One Market Trades the Headline, the Other Trades the Deadline
The two markets are answering different questions.
Oil futures have to react immediately to changes in the probability of war, supply disruption and diplomacy. That is why Brent moved sharply through Thursday, then slipped again on Friday as traders weighed the possibility of a U.S.-Iran truce.
Polymarket traders are being asked something narrower: will shipping actually return to a defined level by a fixed date?
On that question, September 30 is effectively priced out. Even October 31 remains a low-probability outcome.
The futures market therefore sees enough value in the diplomatic channel to move billions of dollars of crude exposure around each new report. The prediction market is saying something more cautious: talks can happen, a framework can emerge and prices can move, while normal Hormuz traffic can still remain a long way off.

sources.text:
American and Iranian negotiators have discussed a phased arrangement that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz while ending the US economic blockade of Iran, according to people familiar with the talks cited by Reuters on 24 September. The reported approach would connect concessions by both sides in stages rather than require one government to yield its principal source of leverage first. A senior Iranian official described relief from the blockade and restored navigation through Hormuz as an initial step. Possible access to frozen Iranian assets was also raised. These are negotiating ideas, and the precise sequence and enforcement terms have not been settled publicly.
The United States wants ships to be able to pass through the strait, a route of major importance to international energy trade. Iran seeks relief from the pressure placed on its economy by the blockade and additional sanctions. Reuters reported that two Iranian sources, two regional officials and two Western diplomatic sources described a persistent obstacle: neither side wants to make its concession first without assurance that the other will follow.
The White House portrayed Washington as holding a strong negotiating position. An official said President Donald Trump remained open to talks under suitable circumstances while maintaining economic pressure on Iran. The official’s claims about the blockade’s effects are the administration’s assessment, not an independently established measure of the Iranian economy. Trump has publicly suggested a deal might follow the 3 November US midterm elections.
A separate issue is Iran’s proposal for fees on traffic through Hormuz. Regional sources told Reuters Tehran could move that demand out of the principal arrangement and into a side attachment, while Gulf governments have rejected payment for transit. That reported flexibility would be temporary and would not amount to Iran abandoning its position over administration of the waterway. Gulf leaders have also pressed for freedom of navigation and for the wider confrontation to be settled politically.
The diplomatic effort follows earlier attempts at a temporary understanding that did not end the conflict. On 22 September, a senior Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran could reopen Hormuz within seven days if the United States reduced military pressure and lifted its blockade. That was the official’s conditional account; it was not a confirmed US-Iran agreement. Iran’s public positions and reported private proposals need to be distinguished as the talks continue.
The negotiations have unfolded alongside the UN General Assembly in New York, where leaders have discussed the war and the disruption of shipping. A phased deal would need to specify when vessels could again use Hormuz and when the US blockade would end. As of the latest reporting, those reciprocal steps remained under discussion, with no announced timetable for implementation.

sources.news_title: US and Iran Explore Phased Deal to Reopen Strait of Hormuz as Oil Prices Fall
sources.text:
- US and Iranian negotiators are exploring a phased agreement that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz and lift Washington's economic blockade of Iran, putting the critical oil route at the center of renewed diplomatic efforts.
US and Iranian negotiators are exploring a phased path toward ending the nearly seven-month conflict that would see Iran reopen the Strait of Hormuz while the US lifts its economic blockade of Iranian ports, according to people familiar with the discussions.
The talks are taking place in New York on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, with Qatar helping mediate, Bloomberg reported. A person familiar with the discussions said both sides were pushing for a potential breakthrough after previously rejecting similar arrangements.
The proposal is significant for energy markets because the Strait of Hormuz is one of the world's most important oil chokepoints. Before the current conflict, the waterway handled roughly 20 million barrels of oil per day, equivalent to about one-fifth of global petroleum liquids consumption, according to the US Energy Information Administration.
Oil prices moved lower Friday as traders assessed the possibility that diplomatic progress could eventually restore more normal shipping through the strait.
Why the Strait of Hormuz Matters to Oil Prices
The latest diplomatic discussions come after a volatile week for crude markets. Brent crude settled at $106.60 a barrel Thursday, up 3.4%, while US West Texas Intermediate crude settled at $94.61, up 2.7%, after a missile attack by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement on Saudi Arabia renewed concerns about regional supply disruptions. Prices subsequently retreated as reports of the US-Iran discussions emerged.
Friday trading reflected the competing forces. Brent was recently around $105 a barrel, while WTI was below $93 as markets weighed the possibility of a diplomatic opening against continuing attacks and supply risks.
The importance of Hormuz extends beyond crude oil. The waterway also handles major volumes of liquefied natural gas, particularly exports from Qatar.
Current traffic remains severely disrupted. Reuters reported that only two commodity vessels crossed the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, compared with a pre-conflict average of about 125 large commercial vessels a day. The agency said the strait previously accounted for roughly 20% of the world's daily crude oil and LNG supply.
That disruption means even a diplomatic agreement would not necessarily restore normal energy flows immediately. Shipping companies, insurers and vessel operators would still have to assess whether the security conditions were sufficient for commercial traffic to resume.
What a US-Iran Hormuz Deal Could Look Like
The discussions center on a sequenced agreement rather than an immediate comprehensive settlement. Reuters reported that an Iranian official described the most plausible path as a staged arrangement in which Iran would allow navigation through Hormuz in exchange for the US lifting its economic blockade. Tehran could also seek access to frozen assets.
Iran has separately indicated that it could reopen the strait within a week if Washington eases military pressure and lifts the blockade. Reuters reported that Tehran had already submitted a proposal through intermediaries. The two sides, however, remain divided over who should make the first concession.
Iran wants sanctions and the blockade eased, while Washington is seeking unrestricted passage through the waterway. Gulf states have also opposed arrangements that would give Iran greater leverage over the strategic shipping route, according to regional officials cited by Reuters.
The diplomatic effort also faces the problem of durability. A previous memorandum reached in June produced a temporary ceasefire before collapsing weeks later, making implementation and enforcement central issues in any new arrangement.
For oil markets, the immediate implication is that geopolitical risk could move in either direction depending on the negotiations.
A credible agreement that restores commercial passage through Hormuz could reduce the supply-risk premium embedded in crude prices. A breakdown in talks or further attacks on energy infrastructure could have the opposite effect.
For now, there is no final US-Iran agreement. The talks represent another diplomatic effort to address the conflict, while the Strait of Hormuz remains the key economic and strategic issue connecting the negotiations to global energy markets.

sources.news_title: ‘Washington, Tehran Exploring Phased Way Out Of War’
sources.text:
• Reports suggest Tehran could reopen Hormuz, may drop toll demand for blockade relief; but ‘neither side wants to move first’
• Gulf states press Trump for post-midterms war strategy; 80 countries call for full restoration of Gulf shipping
• UAE bars Iranian airline flights
WASHINGTON: US and Iranian negotiators in New York are exploring a phased path out of war that would involve Tehran reopening the Strait of Hormuz and Washington lifting its economic blockade of Iran, sources close to the talks said.
The strait, through which a fifth of the world’s oil passes, has become the central bargaining chip in efforts to end the war. Iran wants relief from a blockade that is strangling its economy; Washington wants free passage restored for ships on the vital oil route that Tehran has kept closed.
Talks are complicated by a familiar diplomatic problem: neither side wants to move first.
Two Iranian sources, two regional officials and two Western diplomats said the most workable option now on the table was a staged arrangement — Iran allowing ships through Hormuz in return for an end to the blockade and, potentially, access to frozen assets.
“One way forward would be to solve the crisis in stages. The first would be to end the blockade and reopen Hormuz,” a senior Iranian official said on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
Such a deal would require Donald Trump to accept another interim arrangement, after a previous understanding collapsed in July. The US president has suggested a fuller agreement might only be reached after November’s midterm elections. A senior European official said Iranian negotiators arrived in New York “with a very long list of demands”.
The White House, for its part, has shown little urgency. “Iran is desperate for a deal, President Trump holds all the cards and will make whatever decision is best for the United States,” a White House official said, adding that “crushing sanctions” and “one of the most successful blockades in history” had left Tehran “completely broke”.
Trump, the official suggested, was content to let an “inevitable Iranian collapse” continue rather than be rushed into concessions.
Dennis Ross, a former US negotiator, put the chances of a deal before the midterms at roughly 30 per cent, though he noted both sides had reasons to want an agreement sooner rather than later.
“The blockade is what’s really squeezing the Iranians. It’s strangling them,” he said. A pre-election deal could suit Trump too, easing Gulf tensions and helping bring down petrol prices at home. After the vote, Ross said, the president may feel freer to escalate pressure or consider military options.
Tehran, meanwhile, is hedging. Even as it explores a diplomatic exit, Iran is preparing for the possibility of renewed conflict, accusing Washington of using the blockade and the threat of force as instruments of coercion.
“Our fingers are on the trigger,” the senior Iranian official said. “The Americans know what they need to do but, because of their excessive demands, the chances of diplomacy resolving this are extremely low.”
Regional sources said Iran was prepared to drop, or at least set aside, its demand for transit fees on shipping through Hormuz in order to prioritise ending the blockade.
“Iran is not primarily focused on imposing tolls in Hormuz but on preserving its administrative control of the waterway,” the senior official said. “Iran may be willing to defer the toll issue, but they are not going to give up administrative control of the strait.”
At the heart of the diplomacy in New York is a fundamental tension. Washington wants pressure to produce concessions, Tehran wants pressure removed before making them, and the Gulf states want the conflict resolved without allowing the region’s strategic waterways to become enduring bargaining chips.
In a separate meeting in New York, Gulf leaders pressed Trump for clarity on his strategy beyond the midterms, including whether Washington would resume military action if Iran refused to negotiate.
They made clear their rejection of any Iranian control over Hormuz, insisting freedom of navigation be restored and that the strait must not become a tool of coercion — while also urging de-escalation, reflecting Gulf states’ desire to stay out of further confrontation.
“It’s still not clear what Trump’s endgame is, or what the alternative to the pressure campaign would be,” said Ebtessam al-Ketbi, president of the Emirates Policy Center in Abu Dhabi.
“The Iranians, by contrast, know what they want. They’re reshaping the regional landscape through Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb with a clear objective, while Washington has yet to define its roadmap.”
Alan Eyre, another former US negotiator, warned that the blockade’s pressure could backfire: rather than softening its position, he said, Tehran was more likely to escalate, believing that any sign of weakness would prove fatal to the regime.
Adding to the diplomatic pressure, a coalition of 80 countries called at the UN on Thursday for the full restoration of maritime navigation in the Gulf.
“We call for the full restoration of navigational rights and principles without delay,” said Bahrain’s Foreign Minister Abdullatif bin Rashid al-Zayani, reading a joint statement to journalists.
UAE suspends Iranian airline flights
In a further sign of tightening pressure, the United Arab Emirates announced on Thursday that it would no longer accept flights operated by Iranian carriers, aligning itself with US sanctions targeting Iran’s aviation sector.
Dubai has long been a key destination for Iranian airlines, serving multiple daily flights and a large Iranian community with close business ties to the emirate.
The UAE’s General Civil Aviation Authority said the suspension was “based on the US sanctions imposed on Iranian airlines preventing them from using airports around the world”.
The UAE, which was hit by thousands of Iranian missiles and drones early in the war, suspended trade and financial exchanges with Iran last month.
On Wednesday its central bank blocked transactions with Iran’s Bank Melli, citing breaches of money-laundering, terrorism-financing and arms-proliferation rules.
One passenger told AFP an Iran Airtour flight from Tehran to Dubai was cancelled shortly before departure on Thursday, after tickets had already been issued.
Washington imposed sanctions on Iran’s aviation sector in early September, giving airlines until Wednesday to comply — including by halting the refuelling of Iranian aircraft — or risk being cut off from the dollar-based financial system.
Iran’s main carriers were forced to cancel international flights this week as neighbouring states adopted similar restrictions; Turkmenistan turned back a flight from Tehran to Dushanbe on Thursday, an Iranian aviation official said, because it had not authorised the airline to fly.
A handful of smaller Iranian carriers continue to operate abroad, notably to Armenia and to China, which has declined to follow Washington’s sanctions.

Bitcoin Returns Above $84K as U.S., Iran Discuss Hormuz Deal
Bitcoin traded near $84,200 at the time of writing after recovering from Tuesday’s drop toward $83,000.
The rebound came as U.S. and Iranian negotiators discussed a phased arrangement that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end Washington’s economic blockade of Iran.
$83,000 → $84,200
Recovered part of Tuesday’s sell-off
Below $1.45 → $1.53
Back above a closely watched round level
Hormuz access ↔ blockade relief
A framework under discussion, not a deal
What changed after Tuesday’s sell-off?
Tuesday left crypto traders with the same problem that has hung over markets for months: the Strait of Hormuz remained a live source of energy and geopolitical risk, while the United States continued to squeeze Iran economically.
Wednesday brought a more specific diplomatic signal. Reuters reported that negotiators in New York are exploring a staged path out of the conflict. Under the first stage, Iran would permit navigation through Hormuz and the U.S. would lift its economic blockade. Tehran could also gain access to frozen assets.
That does not amount to an agreement. But it is more substantial than another general call for talks because it identifies the exchange each side is considering. Iran’s control over access to Hormuz would be traded, at least initially, for relief from the pressure Washington has placed on its economy.
The proposed formula leaves the hardest disputes for later
A phased arrangement would allow both governments to deal with the immediate impasse without pretending that every issue has been solved. The first phase would focus on shipping and the blockade. The broader political and security disputes would remain for later negotiations.
The structure matters because the two sides do not need to trust each other on every issue at once. They only need to decide whether the first exchange can be carried out without leaving either side exposed.
Reopening Hormuz may not mean the same thing to both sides
The word “reopen” sounds straightforward. It is not.
Washington wants free passage for commercial shipping. Tehran has signalled that ending the blockade is its priority, but it has also sought to preserve a role in how traffic through the strait is managed. Reuters reported that Iran may be willing to move its demand for transit fees outside the main agreement, while Gulf states have rejected any arrangement that gives Tehran lasting control over the route.
A September 23 assessment by Critical Threats Project and the Institute for the Study of War made the same distinction: Iran’s reference to reopening the strait could mean allowing more commercial traffic under an Iranian-managed system, rather than giving up its claimed authority over shipping.
That is why this report should not be treated as a clean end to the Hormuz problem. The first stage could lower immediate pressure while leaving the central dispute over control of the waterway unresolved.
Crypto recovered, but traders are not pricing a finished settlement
Bitcoin’s return above $84,000 shows that Tuesday’s selling did not develop into a deeper breakdown. Ethereum traded near $2,676, XRP recovered to about $1.53, Solana moved back toward $116.80 and Hyperliquid’s HYPE traded above $93.
The market move should not be reduced to a simple cause-and-effect claim. No official statement confirmed a deal, and crypto had already begun to stabilize after Tuesday’s decline.
Still, the report changes the backdrop. Traders are no longer weighing only the risk that the Hormuz dispute worsens. They are also weighing a concrete, if fragile, route toward easing it. That is enough to matter during a recovery, even before either government publicly accepts the framework.
The July failure is the part markets cannot ignore
There is a reason the report describes a phased arrangement rather than a final settlement. A previous understanding between the U.S. and Iran broke down in July. The problem was not the lack of a first announcement; it was the unresolved terms that followed.
That history makes the next question more important than Wednesday’s headline: who acts first?
Washington wants Iran to restore navigation before it gives up the pressure created by the blockade. Tehran wants relief before it abandons its strongest bargaining tool. Until one side accepts that risk, the framework remains an outline rather than a catalyst with lasting market consequences.
What would turn the report into a real market development?
1. Public confirmation: A statement from Washington or Tehran that they accept the same first-stage terms.
2. A timetable: Details on when the blockade would ease and when commercial traffic could resume.
3. Evidence on the water: A sustained improvement in shipping through Hormuz, rather than another temporary diplomatic opening.
Bitcoin’s rebound shows that the market is willing to reverse part of Tuesday’s risk-off move when diplomacy produces a specific proposal. But the proposal only becomes meaningful when one side gives up leverage first, and the other side proves that its concession will be met.

“Until our conditions are met, the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened and we will not negotiate,” Rezaei said, according to Iran’s state-run IRNA.
He added that Washington would first have to restore the trust of the Iranian people before Tehran would consider resuming negotiations.
Preliminary data showed that 10 cargo vessels passed through the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, compared with seven a day earlier. However, the figure remained below the 10-day average of around 17 vessels.
The data could be revised as some ships switch off their transponders while sailing.
US Central Command said its forces had redirected 115 commercial vessels as of September 23 while enforcing what it called America’s “steel wall blockade”.

The development comes amid heightened tensions surrounding the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for global energy shipments.
Iran has also indicated that the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed until its conditions are addressed. The country is seeking assurances from the United States regarding the waterway, along with measures aimed at rebuilding trust between the two sides
Tehran considers guarantees over the Strait an important part of any future negotiations.
The reported deadline adds another layer to ongoing tensions between Iran and the United States. Any agreement on the conditions could determine whether diplomatic talks resume and whether the situation surrounding the Strait of Hormuz changes. Further developments are expected as the five-day period progresses.
